passage: "Aparna, got a minute?" Rukmini pulled a chair up to Aparna's desk. "Sure. What's up?" "The client deck on Tuesday. The pricing model on slide four was mine. You presented it as your team's." Aparna's smile faded. "I... didn't think it mattered whose." "It matters to me. I shared it because we're on the same side, and I still want to be. But I need the credit when it's mine." A long pause. "You're right. I'll email the client team today and correct it." "Thank you." The next week Aparna's team was stuck on a forecasting sheet. Rukmini stopped by. "Want me to look at it with you?" Aparna blinked. "After last week?" "You fixed it. We're square."

qa.q: Which slide had Rukmini's pricing model?
qa.a: Slide four.

qa.q: What does Aparna's 'After last week?' suggest Aparna was feeling?
qa.a: Aparna was surprised and perhaps still embarrassed, not expecting Rukmini to help again so soon.

qa.q: What choices did Rukmini make, first about the deck and then the next week?
qa.a: Rukmini named the lost credit plainly and asked for it, then offered help once Aparna corrected it, avoiding both silence and a grudge.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had simply stopped sharing with Aparna?
qa.a: Aparna's team would lose a helpful colleague, and the two teams might drift into mutual distrust instead of working together.

grounding: A young professional who shared work openly calls out a colleague's taking of credit plainly, and cooperates again once the colleague corrects it.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: I'm Irfan, and I freelance as a designer. When Pooja from the print shop down the lane first sent me work, I didn't haggle; I did it on time and did it well. She paid on time too. We traded favours for a year: I fixed her menus for free, she printed my cards at cost. Then she took on a rush job and handed my design to someone else to tweak, without asking, and billed it as her own. I didn't go silent or trash her online. I walked in and said, "That was my design. I'd have helped if you'd asked. You can't do that again." She looked embarrassed, apologised, and paid me for it that week. I went back to trading favours. Last month she sent me three new clients.

qa.q: What did Irfan fix for Pooja for free?
qa.a: Her menus.

qa.q: What did Irfan want Pooja to understand by walking in to speak?
qa.a: Irfan stayed calm but firm, wanting Pooja to understand that the design was Irfan's, that help was there if asked, and that doing it again would not be okay.

qa.q: Which of Irfan's choices kept the relationship going after the breach?
qa.a: Naming the problem plainly in person instead of going silent or complaining online, then returning to trading favours once Pooja apologised and paid.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Irfan after that conversation?
qa.a: Pooja may respect Irfan as fair but firm, which may be why she later sent three new clients.

grounding: A young freelancer cooperates first, calls out a partner's misuse of their work plainly, and forgives once she makes it right, keeping a good partnership.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: Supervisor's note, 30 September. Written by Chaitanya. Pradeep, twenty-four, has handled his first year with the warehouse team well. From day one he shared his order forecasts early and helped them plan, though that isn't strictly his job. They returned it: faster dispatches, early warnings about stock. In August their lead, Mr Bose, quietly blamed Pradeep's forecast for a late shipment that was really a warehouse error. Pradeep didn't sulk or start holding his forecasts back. He sent a short, plain email with dates showing where the delay happened and asked for the record to be corrected. Mr Bose called him, admitted it, and fixed the record. Pradeep went straight back to sharing forecasts. The two teams now work together better than any pair on this floor.

qa.q: Who quietly blamed Pradeep's forecast for the late shipment?
qa.a: Mr Bose, the warehouse team's lead.

qa.q: What did Pradeep likely feel when he was blamed, and what shows he kept a cool head?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and annoyed at being wrongly blamed, but he sent a short, plain email with dates rather than sulking.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do after Mr Bose admitted the error, and why was that wise?
qa.a: He went straight back to sharing forecasts, forgiving the slip so the teams didn't fall into mutual punishment.

qa.q: How might Mr Bose see Pradeep after the email?
qa.a: Mr Bose likely respects Pradeep more for being direct but fair, and trusts that Pradeep won't hold a grudge.

grounding: A young professional cooperates first with another team, calls out an unfair blame plainly with evidence, and resumes cooperation once it is corrected.

passage:
Thursday, 11 pm

Today Afreen covered my site visit in Thane without being asked, because I had fever. Writing it down so I remember how we got here.

When I joined in June, I shared my checklists with her on day one, no conditions. She shared her drawings back. Good start.

Then in August she skipped her two agreed site visits and I did them. I didn't sulk or skip mine to get even. I just said, "Afreen, I did your visits twice. That's not our deal. I need you to do yours." She went quiet, then said, "You're right. It was a bad month. It won't happen again." It didn't.

So I let it go completely. No keeping score.

And now she's the one standing on a muddy site at eight in the morning for me. Glad I didn't give up on her in August.
- Zubin

qa.q: Why did Afreen cover Zubin's site visit today?
qa.a: Because Zubin had fever.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel about Afreen skipping her visits in August, and how was it handled?
qa.a: Zubin was clearly bothered, saying it was not their deal, but chose to speak plainly instead of sulking or getting even.

qa.q: Which of Zubin's choices kept the partnership going?
qa.a: Saying the problem clearly without punishing her, and then letting it go fully once she corrected it, gave Afreen a way back without letting Zubin be used.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Zubin after the August conversation?
qa.a: She may respect Zubin for being honest without holding a grudge, which makes her want to return the help, as she did today.

grounding: A young professional cooperates first, calls out a colleague's lapse plainly, and forgives once she corrects it, which keeps the partnership strong.

passage:
Baljeet: Kiran, saw your board. 30% off all weekend?
Kiran: yeah, trying something
Baljeet: we agreed in March, no weekend price cuts on this street. I kept my side
Kiran: I know. sales were bad this month 😔
Baljeet: I get that. but half my regulars walked past to you today. you could have told me first
Kiran: that's fair. I should have
Baljeet: so what now?
Kiran: board comes down tonight. back to normal prices tomorrow
Baljeet: ok. then we're good 👍
Kiran: really? just like that?
Baljeet: you fixed it. and I have more cake orders on Sunday than I can bake. want to take a few?
Kiran: seriously? thank you 🙏
Baljeet: just talk to me next time

qa.q: How much discount did Kiran put on the board?
qa.a: Kiran put 30% off all weekend.

qa.q: What does Kiran's 'really? just like that?' suggest about how Kiran feels?
qa.a: Kiran seems surprised and relieved, expecting Baljeet to stay angry rather than forgive so quickly.

qa.q: What does Baljeet's approach get right?
qa.a: Baljeet points out the broken agreement plainly, accepts the fix at once, and then offers cake orders, so the deal is protected without an endless grudge.

qa.q: How would things change if Baljeet had put up a bigger discount in reply?
qa.a: The two cafes might keep cutting prices against each other, and both would lose money instead of sharing customers and extra orders.

grounding: A young cafe owner who cooperated first calls out a neighbour's price cut plainly, forgives when it is corrected, and returns kindness with kindness.
